name: Lyndal Roper
specialization: Gender, body, and fantasy in early modern German witchcraft

major_works.title: Witch Craze: Terror and Fantasy in Baroque Germany
major_works.significance: Psychoanalytic approach to witchcraft focusing on embodied fantasy, generativity, and aging

major_works.title: Oedipus and the Devil: Witchcraft, Sexuality, and Religion in Early Modern Europe
major_works.significance: Essays developing psychoanalytic and gender approaches to early modern religion and witchcraft

major_works.title: The Holy Household: Women and Morals in Reformation Augsburg
major_works.significance: Foundational study of gender and the Reformation in Augsburg

core_argument: Witchcraft accusations emerged from deep psychic and social anxieties around generativity, the female body, and aging. Post-Freudian analysis reveals that witch confessions and accusations were shaped by unconscious fantasies about motherhood, infanticide, and bodily harm, grounded in real social tensions between older and younger women.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Trial records, interrogation transcripts, confession narratives from Augsburg and Bavaria
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Psychological and somatic content of witch confessions; social relationships between accusers and accused
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Narrative analysis of confession content; gender and age demographics of accused and accusers
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Psychoanalytic and social-bodily; individual psychology embedded in communal structures

key_contributions.claim: Witch fantasies were rooted in bodily experience — particularly around lactation, infanticide, and aging — rather than purely in theological doctrine
key_contributions.implication: Witch trials cannot be understood purely as intellectual or legal history; they reflect deep somatic anxieties

key_contributions.claim: Accusations typically ran between older post-menopausal women and younger women with infants, reflecting tension over reproductive capacity
key_contributions.implication: The social profile of witchcraft accusation reveals structured intergenerational conflict rather than random persecution

key_contributions.claim: Psychoanalytic categories (projection, fantasy, unconscious) can be applied to historical evidence without anachronism if grounded in period-specific somatic beliefs
key_contributions.implication: Opens productive dialogue between historical method and psychological theory

reception_and_critique.major_influences: Feminist theory, psychoanalytic theory (Freud, Melanie Klein), social history of early modern Germany
criticisms: Psychoanalytic framework seen as anachronistic by some historians
Hutton and others question whether projecting modern psychological categories onto early modern minds is valid
Scope limited largely to German (especially Augsburg/Bavarian) material

historiographical_significance: Roper's work fundamentally shifted witchcraft historiography toward the body and psyche, challenging purely intellectual and social-structural explanations. Her integration of gender theory with close reading of confessional documents opened new analytical possibilities. Her position as Regius Professor of History at Oxford signals her central standing in the field.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
